subject: paediatrics
title: Neonatal Bacterial Pathogens, Rubella and Cytomegalovirus

steps.tx: The predominant bacterial pathogen responsible for neonatal sepsis in low- and middle-income countries is **multidrug resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae**. Characterized by rapid cross-transmission via health worker hands in crowded neonatal units, Klebsiella strains produce extended-spectrum beta-lactamases and carbapenemases, presenting with explosive septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and extensive sclerema neonatorum.
steps.say: Multidrug-resistant Klebsiella is the leading cause of neonatal sepsis in developing country nurseries.

rows: Gram-positive coccus in pairs and chains
Dominant in India and LMIC nurseries
Uniformly susceptible to penicillin and ampicillin

steps.tx: In Western healthcare settings, the leading bacterial cause of early-onset sepsis is **Group B Streptococcus**, also known as Streptococcus agalactiae. Maternal rectovaginal colonization at thirty-six to thirty-seven weeks gestation permits ascending transmission during labor. Universal maternal screening and intrapartum intravenous penicillin prophylaxis administered at least four hours prior to delivery reduce early-onset GBS disease by eighty percent.
steps.say: Intrapartum intravenous penicillin prophylaxis prevents vertical transmission of Group B Streptococcus.

left.title: Universal Screening Protocol
points: Rectovaginal swab at 36 to 37 weeks gestation

right.title: Intrapartum Prophylaxis
points: First dose at least 4 hours before delivery
Eliminates vertical transmission to the newborn

steps.tx: The laboratory answers two questions about this nursery pathogen on the same day. The Gram film shows plump Gram negative bacilli wrapped in a thick capsule, the **Klebsiella** morphology behind much neonatal sepsis in low resource units. Around the antibiotic discs, shrunken or absent zones then warn of ESBL or carbapenemase production, steering empiric therapy away from cephalosporins that would silently fail.
steps.say: Gram stain shows encapsulated Gram negative Klebsiella rods. Disc zones shrinking around key antibiotics warn of ESBL or carbapenemase production and redirect empiric therapy.

vis.alt: Gram stained smear of plump Gram negative rods with pale capsular halos beside an agar plate carrying antibiotic discs and zones of inhibition.
vis.caption: Gram stain of encapsulated Klebsiella pneumoniae with disc susceptibility testing for ESBL and carbapenemase production. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Congenital intrauterine infections transmitted vertically from mother to fetus are grouped under the **TORCH complex designation**. Comprising Toxoplasma gondii, Others like Syphilis and Varicella, Rubella virus, Cytomegalovirus, and Herpes simplex virus, these pathogens cause a shared spectrum of fetal damage including intrauterine growth restriction, microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss, and hepatosplenomegaly.
steps.say: The TORCH pathogens share clinical features including growth failure, microcephaly, and organomegaly.

vis.alt: Diagnostic triads and clinical features of the TORCH congenital infections.
vis.caption: Diagnostic triads and clinical hallmarks of congenital STORCH intrauterine infections. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Maternal primary rubella infection during the critical first trimester causes **congenital rubella syndrome**. The virus infects vascular endothelial cells, causing obliterative vasculitis and arrest of organogenesis. Classic clinical diagnosis depends on recognizing the historic Gregg triad: sensorineural hearing impairment, congenital nuclear cataracts with microphthalmia, and congenital structural heart disease.
steps.say: Congenital rubella presents with the Gregg triad of cataracts, deafness, and congenital heart disease.

rows: Red reflex examination and ophthalmology referral
Patent ductus arteriosus, peripheral pulmonary stenosis
Echocardiography demonstrating ductal shunt or stenosis

steps.tx: Dermal extramedullary hematopoiesis creates the striking **blueberry muffin rash** in congenital rubella and cytomegalovirus. Bluish-red, non-blanching maculopapules distribute across the face, trunk, and extremities within hours of birth. The lesions represent persistent dermal erythropoiesis compensatory to severe intrauterine anemia and reticuloendothelial viral destruction, resolving spontaneously over several weeks.
steps.say: Blueberry muffin lesions represent dermal extramedullary erythropoiesis from severe intrauterine infection.

left.title: Dermal Blueberry Muffin Lesions
points: Histology reveals islands of erythroblasts and myelocytes
Resolves spontaneously as medullary hematopoiesis recovers

steps.tx: The most common congenital viral infection worldwide is **congenital cytomegalovirus infection**, occurring in approximately one percent of all live births. While over eighty-five percent of infected infants are asymptomatic at birth, ten to fifteen percent develop severe systemic cytomegalic inclusion disease featuring microcephaly, extensive periventricular calcifications, chorioretinitis, petechial rash, and profound sensorineural deafness.
steps.say: Cytomegalovirus is the most common congenital viral infection, causing microcephaly and calcifications.

rows: Leading non-genetic cause of childhood deafness
Petechiae and jaundice resolving in infancy

steps.tx: The pathognomonic intracranial neuroimaging hallmark of congenital cytomegalovirus is **periventricular calcification patterns**. Viral tropism for the rapidly dividing subependymal germinal matrix surrounding the lateral ventricles produces severe necrotizing ependymitis followed by dense dystrophic calcification along the ventricular margins, in contrast to the diffuse parenchymal calcifications seen in congenital toxoplasmosis.
steps.say: Cytomegalovirus produces distinctive calcifications outlining the margins of the lateral ventricles.

right.title: Toxoplasmosis Calcifications
points: Involves cortex, subcortex, and basal ganglia

steps.tx: Definitive diagnosis requires **urine or saliva CMV PCR** obtained within the first three weeks of life. Detection of viral DNA after three weeks cannot differentiate congenital transmission from benign postnatally acquired breast milk infection. Symptomatic neonates are treated with oral valganciclovir for six months, which substantially prevents progressive hearing deterioration and neurodevelopmental decline.
steps.say: CMV PCR must be performed within three weeks of birth, with oral valganciclovir preserving hearing.

rows: Saliva or urine PCR within 21 days
High oral bioavailability, replaces IV ganciclovir
Weekly absolute neutrophil count and liver panel
